content: This guide acknowledges the contributions of several individuals to its development. Elena Altieri coordinated the drafting and production of the document. Tom Hundley served as the editor. Adrian Brown, Geoffrey Cain, Tom Hundley, Annie Kelly, Guilherme Paranaiba Gouveia, and Subhendu Ray contributed their respective sections. Kidist Bartolomeos, Marina Carter, Roberto Colombo, Nathalie Draisin, Paul Garwood, Rebecca Ivers, Meleckidzedeck Khayesi, Etienne Krug, Callie Long, Richard Mills, Evelyn Murphy, Victor Pavarino, Margie Peden, Carolyn Robinson, Eugenia Rodriguez, Hala Sakr, Laura Sminkey, Tamitza Toroyan, Joe Weber, and Elena Yurasova reviewed the drafts. Catherine Allen, Sarika Bansal, Sandra Damiani, Banung Ou, and Piyush Tewari provided additional contributions. Hélène Dufays supported the document’s production, and Elizabeth Heseltine edited the final draft. This guide is the result of four years of work with media on road safety in ten countries. Between 2011 and 2014, WHO engaged over 1,300 journalists through road safety workshops. The aim was to increase their interest, knowledge, and understanding of this complex issue. The ultimate goal was not just more stories but more comprehensive and compelling stories about road traffic injuries and their impact on people’s lives. Every day, approximately 3,400 people die in road traffic crashes worldwide. These events often make the news, but the full stories behind them—who, why, how, and how they could have been avoided—are rarely well-developed. Road traffic deaths and injuries, however, are preventable. The United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety 2011–2020 highlights effective interventions, primarily from high-income countries, that can change road user behavior, improve roads and vehicles, and enhance emergency care systems. Efforts are being made to bring these experiences to lowand middle-income countries, where over 90% of road traffic deaths occur. Far too many people die unnecessarily on the world’s roads, even in high-income countries. While the knowledge to prevent these deaths exists, it rarely makes its way into the news. This guide aims to change that. It provides reporters with new angles, examples of stories and projects from around the world, and tips from editors, reporters, and public health experts. The goal is to see more in-depth stories on road safety in the media and to witness a new era of road safety journalism focused on solutions and saving lives. Dr. Etienne Krug, Director of the Department for Management of Noncommunicable Diseases, Disability, Violence, and Injury Prevention at WHO, emphasizes that road traffic fatalities are not random, isolated accidents but a public health crisis with catastrophic consequences for victims and societies. Journalists, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, have the opportunity to educate their audiences, increase public awareness, and influence policymakers to address this issue. Lowand middle-income countries account for about 50% of the world’s vehicle traffic but nearly 90% of traffic deaths. In regions like Africa and parts of Asia, road crashes are often dismissed as inevitable costs of economic progress or acts of fate. Journalists can challenge this perspective by highlighting the preventable nature of these tragedies and advocating for solutions. Reporting on road safety requires more than familiarity with driving statistics. Journalists must delve into the complex interplay of factors leading to road traffic fatalities. Road safety is a broader story than a single fatal crash buried in the pages of a newspaper. It is a public health issue that intersects with global development, poverty alleviation, and education. This guide is designed to help journalists understand the full dimensions of road safety and write more in-depth stories on the subject. It provides tips for pitching stories to editors, using statistics effectively, and finding human-interest angles. Road safety is not just a policy or safety issue; it is a story about people, often the poorest and most vulnerable members of society. The ripple effects of road traffic crashes can be catastrophic, pushing households into poverty and leaving survivors without compensation or the ability to work. The guide also highlights the importance of making road safety a priority in post-2015 development targets. It emphasizes the need for journalists to connect road safety to broader development goals and to present it as a critical public health issue affecting millions of lives.
